motion: The special U.S.-Saudi relationship has outlived its usefulness.

dropped_turns.speaker: PRO
dropped_turns.text: Hina, I am answering your access point: private channels matter, but they do not require a special political bond. By separating necessary contact from automatic favor, Washington gains credibility and bargaining power.

dropped_turns.speaker: CON
dropped_turns.text: Michelle, what tells an anxious partner that Washington remains reliable if it downgrades this relationship while dangers are rising? If trust is weakened first, why would your promised leverage become stronger afterward?

dropped_turns.speaker: PRO
dropped_turns.text: When officials face abuses and Washington answers with public concern but unchanged special treatment, affected families see words without consequences. A normal relationship could preserve contact while withholding favors, proving privilege has outlived usefulness.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Welcome to tonight's debate. The motion is whether the special U.S.-Saudi relationship has outlived its usefulness. Michelle supports the motion, while Hina opposes it. Each debater has thirty seconds for an opening, then two and a half minutes of crossfire, and thirty seconds to close; I will give a ten-second cue before each time expires.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: This relationship once traded security cooperation for dependable energy access, but that bargain now traps both sides in habits neither can defend. Washington keeps offering exceptional treatment despite repeated clashes over values and regional choices. A partnership can continue without being special. The question is whether privileged ties still serve American interests today, not yesterday.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds, ten seconds.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: The answer is no. Ordinary diplomacy can protect shared needs while withholding blank checks, and it lets Washington cooperate selectively without confusing access with approval. Keeping an outdated special status makes reform harder-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Your time is up. Thank you. Hina.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Michelle calls the tie a blank check, but it is leverage: regular contact lets Washington press concerns while protecting shared security interests in a volatile region.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: But contact without consequences is not leverage-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Let her answer it.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: That protection is not automatic; it rests on mutual interests, and ending special ties would reduce the access needed to shape conduct when crises arrive.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Well, now ten.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Preserving a working special partnership gives Washington more choices, not fewer, when dangers spread. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: That concludes Round One. Now, we move on to Round Two. And Round Two is where the debaters address one another directly. Two and a half minutes on the clock, starting the moment I stop talking.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Michelle, I am answering your blank-check point: a relationship is useful precisely because it creates channels for pressure when disagreement is sharp. Removing its special character abandons leverage, not dependence.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: When cooperation is available through ordinary agreements, exceptional status adds little but political cost. If leaders know protection continues after defiance, calling the tie special shields them from meaningful consequences.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Imagine a sudden threat to commercial shipping: trusted military coordination and direct calls can prevent a wider clash before it reaches families and markets. That safeguard proves the relationship still serves.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: I grant direct contact can calm an immediate crisis. But the main issue is whether permanent privilege buys more than ordinary coordination, and it rewards refusal rather than change, so the special relationship has outlived usefulness.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Your weakest claim is that ordinary coordination can replace a trusted framework. In a crisis, improvised channels lack shared expectations, and losing them makes misunderstanding more likely while giving Washington less influence.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: If misunderstanding grows during an evacuation, families need clear routes, trusted hotlines, and practiced coordination between crews. Those preparations matter because confusion at a crowded terminal can turn fear into avoidable injury.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: No, the special us-saudi relationship has outlived its usefulness, the special us-saudi relationship has outlived its usefulness. Those are the key words.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: On whether the special U.S.-Saudi relationship has outlived its usefulness, the answer is yes: useful contact does not require privileged status. Ordinary cooperation preserves necessary communication while allowing consequences when conduct conflicts with American interests.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Michelle, if exceptional access is removed during a sudden regional crisis, who will coordinate urgent protection for civilians and commerce? Your ordinary arrangements cannot create trust instantly, so why discard a proven channel?

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: No foreign partnership deserves permanent privilege merely because it once solved a problem. American cooperation should be judged by present conduct and interests, not ceremonial labels or old expectations of protection.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I agree labels alone cannot excuse harmful conduct. Yet you treat special status as automatic protection, when it is a platform for bargaining; throwing it away would leave Washington facing crises with fewer tools-

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: But bargaining fails when one side expects protection whatever it does. Why should Washington keep a special promise if ordinary cooperation can handle shared dangers and conditional pressure can defend its interests?

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: It should not keep any unconditional promise, but that is not what this relationship is. Special access lets Washington bargain privately and respond quickly; abandoning it sacrifices influence before testing better terms.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds left, then we go to closings.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Okay, time. And now we move on to Round three. Round three will be closing statements by each debater in turn. Here making her closing statement in support of the motion, Michelle.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: The strongest point is simple: America can keep necessary communication without granting permanent privilege. When a partner expects protection despite harmful choices, the special label removes leverage. Replace exceptional treatment with ordinary, conditional cooperation, and the United States protects its interests and its credibility. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Go ahead. Go ahead, Hina.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Michelle mistakes a useful tool for a blank check. The strongest point is that trusted access gives Washington the ability to press, warn, and coordinate when danger is immediate; ordinary arrangements cannot be rebuilt on demand. That capacity matters most when leaders need answers quickly.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Keep it special, strengthen its terms, and preserve the influence needed to manage shared dangers. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds for last word.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Thank you, Michelle and Hina, for a thoughtful debate. This concludes our discussion of the motion this evening.
